frame: Positions: parsecs from the Sun, J2000 ecliptic axes (x to the J2000 equinox, z to the ecliptic north pole; ICRS rotated by the IAU 1976 obliquity 84381.448"). Velocities: km/s, same axes, heliocentric.
epoch: J2000.0 (JD 2451545.0 TT). Barycentres move in straight lines; members follow the listed Kepler orbits.
orbitModel: Each orbit links two groups of members. Relative position of group 2 about group 1: r = aAu*[(cos E - e) pHat + sqrt(1-e^2) sin E qHat], E - e sin E = 2 pi (JD - tPeriJD) / periodDays. Members of group 1 are displaced by -m2/(m1+m2) r, members of group 2 by +m1/(m1+m2) r (m = total mass of each group). A member position is the system barycentre plus the sum of its displacements over all orbits. pHat, qHat are unit vectors in the J2000 ecliptic frame.

systems.name: Alpha Centauri
systems.note: Hierarchical triple. A and B orbit each other every 79.76 yr (Akeson et al. 2021). Proxima orbits the AB pair at about 8,000-13,000 au. Its orbit here is the osculating Kepler orbit computed from present-day astrometry (Gaia DR3 for Proxima, Akeson et al. 2021 for the AB barycentre) and gravitational-redshift-corrected radial velocities (Kervella et al. 2017), the same method as Kervella et al. 2017. With the newer, larger AB parallax the orbit comes out a little smaller than their published one; both are listed.

Orbit semi-major axis 0.74272 au (Torres et al. 2015: 0.74272 +- 0.00069 au). The ORB6 ephemeris is 180 deg from this model: ORB6 lists Torres et al.'s omega of star A (342.6 deg) as the relative-orbit omega, while the relative orbit of B about A has omega_A + 180 deg, which is what reproduces Torres et al.'s radial-velocity curves.

stars.name: Capella Aa
stars.notes: The cooler, more massive giant, near the end of core helium burning (red clump).

stars.name: Capella Ab
stars.notes: The hotter giant, crossing the Hertzsprung gap; rotates in 8.5 days.

derived.radiusRsun: theta_LD/2 x 11.257 pc (catalogue distance); error excludes the distance error

stars.name: Vega
stars.notes: A fast rotator seen almost pole-on: equator 2.73 R_sun at 8,910 K, poles 2.42 R_sun at 10,070 K. teffK is the surface average.

stars.name: Rigel
stars.notes: Blue supergiant. Its luminosity is not well agreed; 123,000 L_sun is the value de Almeida et al. 2022 adopt as consistent with the Hipparcos parallax (3.78 +- 0.34 mas, 265 pc); their intensity interferometry gives 260 +- 20 pc. No radius or temperature is given here because no source was verified for this file; the catalogue colour temperature applies.

stars.name: Betelgeuse
stars.notes: Distance is uncertain: Hipparcos 2007 gives 6.55 +- 0.83 mas (153 pc), Harper et al. 2017 combine it with radio positions to get 222 (+48 -34) pc, and Joyce et al. 2020 find 168 (+27 -15) pc from seismic and evolutionary modelling. The radius scales with the adopted distance. The star is a semiregular variable (V = 0.0 to 1.6).

stars.name: Altair
stars.notes: Spins at 92% of break-up: 24% wider at the equator than pole to pole, and 1,600 K cooler there (gravity darkening). The mass is an assumed input of the model.

stars.name: Aldebaran

derived.radiusRsun: theta_LD/2 x 20.434 pc (catalogue distance); error excludes the distance error

stars.notes: Mass from evolutionary tracks, uncertain by 43%.

stars.name: Antares

derived.radiusRsun: theta_LD/2 x 169.779 pc (catalogue distance); error excludes the distance error

stars.notes: Radius follows from the angular diameter and the Hipparcos 2007 parallax (5.89 +- 1.00 mas), so it carries a 17% distance uncertainty.

stars.name: Spica
stars.notes: A 4-day double-lined binary; the catalogue has one point for both stars. Values are for the primary; the companion is listed separately.

stars.name: Pollux

derived.radiusRsun: theta_LD/2 x 10.358 pc (catalogue distance); error excludes the distance error

stars.notes: Hosts the giant planet Pollux b (Thestias).

stars.name: Fomalhaut
stars.notes: Surrounded by a dust belt at about 140 au.

stars.name: Deneb
stars.notes: Distance is the main uncertainty. Schiller & Przybilla 2008 adopt 802 +- 66 pc from membership of Cyg OB7; the Hipparcos 2007 parallax (2.31 +- 0.32 mas) implies 433 pc, which the catalogue uses. The radius and luminosity listed here belong with 802 pc.

stars.name: Regulus
stars.notes: Spins at 96% of break-up; equatorial radius 4.21, polar radius 3.22 R_sun. Mass from evolutionary tracks.

stars.name: Polaris
stars.notes: A pulsating Cepheid with a close companion (Polaris Ab, 30-yr orbit). Evans et al. 2024 use the Gaia DR3 parallax of the wide companion Polaris B (136.9 pc); Hipparcos 2007 gives 7.54 +- 0.11 mas (133 pc). No temperature is given here; the catalogue colour temperature applies.

derived.radiusRsun: theta_LD/2 x 3.650 pc (catalogue distance); error excludes the distance error

stars.name: Epsilon Eridani

derived.radiusRsun: theta_LD/2 x 3.219 pc (catalogue distance); error excludes the distance error

stars.notes: A young, active star with a dust disc and a giant planet (AEgir).

stars.name: 51 Pegasi

derived.radiusRsun: theta_LD/2 x 15.518 pc (catalogue distance); error excludes the distance error

stars.notes: First Sun-like star found to host a planet (51 Peg b, Dimidium; Mayor & Queloz 1995). Teff is derived here from the angular diameter and bolometric flux.

stars.name: HR 8799
stars.notes: Host of four directly imaged giant planets. The mass assumes the star is still contracting toward the main sequence (age ~30 Myr).

stars.name: Barnard's Star
stars.notes: Largest proper motion of any star (10.4 arcsec per year). Straight-line motion from its Gaia DR3 astrometry brings it to 1.16 pc from the Sun in about 9,700 years.

stars.name: TRAPPIST-1
stars.notes: Seven Earth-sized planets. Not in AT-HYG (too faint for Tycho-2); added to the catalogue from Gaia DR3.
